transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Cora Vekulman.
Hundreds of thousands of protesters turned down in France over the weekend.
They're angry at the government for failing to address the high cost of living and the
needs of students.
And Pierre's Eleanor Beardsley says there have been similar demonstrations across Europe.
These protests have taken place, you know, like Spain, Portugal, Italy, Albania, and
other countries.
The spark that sets them off is sometimes different.
But what we're seeing, you know, like schools are affordable housing and even corruption.
But what they have in common is they're mostly leaderless.
They're being led by young people who are angry about the world that's being left to
them.
And Pierre's Eleanor Beardsley reporting from Paris.
Voters in the Balkan country of Serbia ousted their longtime leader in elections over the
weekend.
That political movement was also organized by Serbian students and young people.
In the U.S., President Trump will continue his campaign swing today by visiting Mississippi
for a rally.
He'll stump for Republicans in a state that is typically safe for GOP candidates.
Trump was in Michigan yesterday also to campaign, but he spent time there bashing the Michigan
Democratic Senate candidate, calling him a "jihadist."
From member station WDET, Quinn Klinefelter has more.
Trump spent much of his speech blasting Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, calling
his progressive policies, an attempt at a socialist takeover of the nation.
The president barely touched on issues like the high cost of living, tariffs, or the war
in Iran.
Trump did argue increased fuel prices are only a short-term dilemma.
Are you kidding?
I thought gas would be double and triple, and it's a small price to pay for taking a nuclear
weapon away from maniacs.
The rally was on the border with Canada, which Trump claims is "willing to give us anything
to end the current trade war."
For NPR News, I'm Quinn Klinefelter in Detroit.
The Justice Department is planning to send 1,000 election monitors across the country
for the midterm elections.
NPR's Windsor Johnston reports some states say they'll keep a close eye on these monitors.
The Justice Department says its monitors will protect voting rights and help prevent intimidation.
It also denies plans to send armed agents to polling places.
Oregon Secretary of State Tobias Reed says federal observers must follow state rules.
They have to sign our observer agreement and agree to abide by the rules laid out in that
document.
Other states are also setting boundaries; Maine and Nevada have issued guidance on federal
observers' limited authority; Minnesota deployed state employees to shadow federal monitors
during its primary; California has launched a similar program.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
The artificial intelligence company, Anthropic, says its AI model, Claude, got into some Georgia
voter counts without the approval of a human.
Axios first reported on this.
The voter information was already publicly available, but it was also behind a paywall.
Anthropic released its statement yesterday saying the material was limited to Georgia
aggregate voting counts, and it said its AI agent did not access Georgia's voter registration
lists or change or poll any voting records.
Oregon's Communist Party has kicked off its most important meeting this year.
NPR's Jennifer Pack reports from Beijing it's closely watched by observers for clues
on the country's direction and future leadership.
Roughly 300 central committee members will meet behind closed doors this week.
The Chinese public won't hear much of the proceedings until the meeting is wrapped up
Thursday.
And even then, the readout might be full of opaque party terminology.
Chinese Xinhua News Agency says Chinese leader Xi Jinping opened the session Monday presenting
a draft decision on "strengthening full and rigorous party self-governance and perseverance."
Already, Xi has tightened party discipline by continually purging officials for corruption.
The meeting comes at a crucial time.
Next year, Xi is expected to secure an unprecedented fourth term.
Jennifer Pack, NPR News, Beijing.
Tonight is Game 3 of the World Series, the Tampa Bay Rays will host the Milwaukee Brewers.
Milwaukee leads two games to none in the Best of Seven series.
You're listening to NPR.
Want to hear this podcast without sponsor breaks?
Amazon Prime members can listen to NPR News now, sponsor free through Amazon Music.
Or you can also support NPR's vital journalism and get NPR+ at plus.npr.org.
Plus dot NPR dot org.

topics.text: Hundreds of thousands protest in France over cost of living and student needs
Similar leaderless youth-led protests spread across Spain, Portugal, Italy, and Albania
Voters in Serbia oust longtime leader in weekend elections led by students
Trump to rally in Mississippi for Republicans in a typically safe GOP state
Trump's Michigan rally attacks Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as socialist
Justice Department plans 1,000 election monitors for midterms; states set limits
Anthropic says its AI model Claude accessed Georgia aggregate voter counts without approval
China's Communist Party opens closed-door central committee meeting led by Xi Jinping
Tampa Bay Rays host Milwaukee Brewers in World Series Game 3 tonight
